Treatment of OCD: Evidence‑based options, algorithms, and special populations

Overview and stepped-care principles
Across guidelines and meta-analyses, first-line care combines selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) with exposure and response prevention (ERP), a form of cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) that targets compulsions and rituals through graduated exposure and response blocking; this combination generally yields better outcomes than either alone in adults and severe cases, while CBT/ERP monotherapy is first-line for mild to moderate OCD when available and acceptable to the patient <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Prolonged administration of SSRIs is most effective, and better results can be obtained with a SSRI combined with CBT or ERP</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">NICE guidance recommends stepped care; mild symptoms can be offered low-intensity CBT including ERP, and for moderate symptoms, either SSRIs or high-intensity CBT (including ERP); combination therapy is used for severe illness</cite> <cite id="7c705456-0">International guidelines recommend SSRIs, clomipramine, and CBT with ERP as effective treatments for OCD</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Behavioral approaches were sometimes more effective than SSRIs, but combinations are acceptable and not clearly superior; NICE’s stepped approach is broadly supported</cite>.

Evidence for psychotherapies
Randomized trials and meta-analyses consistently show CBT with ERP reduces Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) scores and functional impairment versus controls and is recommended by international guidelines; typical response rates after ERP include substantial reductions to Y-BOCS ≤14 in roughly 60%, with a minority achieving full symptom remission (Y-BOCS ≤7) <cite id="7c705456-0">Guidelines recommend CBT with ERP; meta-analyses support SSRIs and clomipramine as effective, with clomipramine’s tolerability generally worse than SSRIs</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-2">A meta-analysis found psychotherapeutic interventions produced superior outcomes compared to pharmacological treatments, though many pharmacotherapy trials included patients on stable antidepressants, complicating direct comparisons; after ERP, 60% recovered (Y-BOCS ≤14) but only 25% became asymptomatic (Y-BOCS ≤7)</cite>. For children and adolescents, stepped-care models mirror adults: low-intensity CBT/ERP for mild cases and high-intensity CBT/ERP or pharmacotherapy for moderate-to-severe cases, with combination therapy used when needed; evidence suggests behavioral approaches can be as good or better than SSRIs, though combination versus monotherapy superiority remains uncertain <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">NICE recommends stepped care across age groups; evidence indicates behavioral approaches may be more effective than SSRIs, but combination therapy is acceptable and not clearly outperforms monotherapy</cite>.

Pharmacotherapies: SSRIs, tricyclics, and beyond
SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, citalopram/venlafaxine NRIs) are first-line due to efficacy and tolerability; prolonged use is key, and switching among SSRIs can help non-responders. Network meta-analyses and head-to-head trials show clomipramine is effective but not superior to SSRIs overall; clomipramine has more adverse effects (anticholinergic, cardiac, neurologic), favoring SSRIs as first-line, with clomipramine considered when SSRIs fail or in severe cases <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Prolonged SSRI administration is most effective; adding CBT/ERP improves outcomes; for refractory OCD, switching to another SSRI or to clomipramine, or augmenting with an atypical antipsychotic, is recommended</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-1">Clomipramine pioneered OCD pharmacotherapy; newer SSRIs (fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline) are effective and well tolerated; venlafaxine/citalopram efficacy is under investigation; potent SSRIs are first choice; if one SSRI fails, others may help; OCD is often chronic and requires long-term treatment</cite> <cite id="7c705456-0">SSRIs and clomipramine are both significantly more effective than placebo; network meta-analysis found no efficacy advantage of clomipramine over SSRIs; most head-to-head trials found no significant difference in efficacy, but clomipramine had worse tolerability</cite>. For adults not improving on SSRIs, switching to or adding clomipramine, trying another SSRI, or augmenting with an atypical antipsychotic are considered; combining clomipramine with citalopram has also been reported, though evidence is mixed <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">NICE and later reviews recommend: additional CBT of increased intensity, adding an antipsychotic to an SSRI or clomipramine, or combining clomipramine and citalopram for SSRI/clomipramine-resistant OCD; order not specified</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Refractory OCD can be treated by switching to another SSRI or clomipramine, or augmenting with an atypical antipsychotic</cite>.

Combination therapy and augmentation
Guidelines and reviews support combining SSRIs with CBT/ERP as first-line for moderate-to-severe OCD and when comorbidities (e.g., major depression) warrant pharmacotherapy; combination may be preferred over monotherapy in severe cases or with nonadherence, and is commonly used when initial monotherapy fails <cite id="7c705456-0">A combination of SSRIs and CBT is recommended for severe OCD, in the presence of comorbid conditions benefiting from pharmacotherapy, or when monotherapy fails</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Better results are obtained with SSRI plus CBT/ERP compared to either alone</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Combination SSRIs + CBT is acceptable and used for severe illness; behavioral approaches sometimes outperform SSRIs, but combination versus psychotherapy alone superiority is uncertain</cite>. For SSRI-resistant OCD, typical augmentation strategies include atypical antipsychotic augmentation (e.g., risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, haloperidol), though long-term risks and selection of dose/duration remain areas of uncertainty; adding antipsychotics to clomipramine or switching to clomipramine are also options; evidence for adjunct “other medications” (e.g., intravenous antidepressants) is inconsistent <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Refractory OCD can be managed by switching to another SSRI or clomipramine, or augmenting with an atypical antipsychotic; evidence for adding non-antipsychotic medications or IV antidepressants is inconsistent</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">Systematic review/meta-analysis summarizes trials of haloperidol, risperidone, quetiapine, and olanzapine; NICE originally recommended antipsychotic augmentation after CBT/ERP and SSRI/clomipramine trials; current reviews continue to recommend antipsychotics as a class for augmentation, with attention to long-term risks</cite>.

Interventional and neuromodulation options for refractory disease
Several brain stimulation modalities are studied in treatment‑resistant OCD, with the strongest evidence for deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the ventral capsule/ventral striatum (junction with nucleus accumbens) and the subthalamic nucleus, and for repetitive/transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS/dTMS) to the supplementary motor area or orbitofrontal cortex; tDCS may be beneficial with cathodal polarity, while VNS and ECT have less robust evidence (often lacking sham control). Overall, techniques are promising as add-on therapy for severely ill, drug- and behaviorally refractory patients, but heterogeneity, small/underpowered, and inconsistent results limit consensus on targets, parameters, and maintenance strategies <cite id="599423ce-1">Different add-on stimulation techniques could be effective for severely ill, drug/behaviorally refractory OCD; DBS and TMS show best evidence; low-frequency TMS over SMA/OF cortex may be more effective; DBS targets include the accumbens–ventral capsule or subthalamic nucleus; cathodal tDCS may be better than anodal; results are inconsistent</cite> <cite id="599423ce-2">Severe resistant OCD may benefit from noninvasive rTMS/dTMS/tDCS and invasive DBS, VNS, or ECT; no consensus on stimulation sites, parameters, duration, or maintenance; double-blind sham-controlled trials are sparse, with VNS lacking sham-controlled studies</cite>.

Special populations and stepped-climbing care
For children and adolescents, stepped-care models mirror adults: low-intensity CBT/ERP for mild presentations, with high-intensity CBT/ERP and/or pharmacotherapy for moderate-to-severe cases; SSRIs are recommended first-line when available, with attention to safety and monitoring due to suicidality risk; family involvement is often integral, and education about ERP principles (collaborative grading, tolerating anxiety) is emphasized to improve adherence and reduce dropout <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">NICE recommends stepped care for young people; those with mild symptoms can be offered low-intensity CBT including ERP</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Guideline-supported stepped approach is broadly supported; behavioral interventions sometimes more effective than SSRIs; combination therapy used for severe cases</cite>. In adults with mild-to-moderate OCD, CBT/ERP monotherapy is often preferred where feasible; SSRIs remain first-line pharmacotherapy, and combination therapy is reserved for severe illness, comorbid depression, or when psychotherapy access is limited <cite id="7c705456-0">CBT/ERP is recommended across severities; SSRIs plus CBT for severe cases or comorbidity</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Adults with moderate symptoms: SSRIs or high-intensity CBT (including ERP); combination used for severe illness</cite>.

Maintenance, relapse prevention, and stepped-down strategies
OCD frequently requires long-term management to prevent relapse; strategies include gradual reduction of medication dose when stable, maintenance SSRI or CBT skills as needed, and sustained ERP exposure hierarchies with in vivo and cognitive techniques; switching among SSRIs or considering clomipramine may help durable nonresponders; ongoing monitoring for residual insight and belief-based drives (obsessional insight) is recommended alongside symptom scales such as Y-BOCS <cite id="0bfc4231-1">OCD is frequently a chronic condition that requires long-term treatment</cite> <cite id="7c705456-0">CBT education on principles and managing anxiety during ERP is emphasized; insight measures (Y-BOCS Item 11, BABS, OVIS, OBQ) guide monitoring</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Combining SSRI with CBT/ERP is associated with optimal response compared to each alone; refractory cases may switch to clomipramine or augment with antipsychotic</cite>.

Practical sequencing and shared decisions
- Mild to moderate: Offer stepped CBT/ERP, with SSRIs as first-line oral option when available; combine if after an adequate trial one modality is insufficient <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Low-intensity CBT/ERP for mild; moderate cases can receive SSRIs or high-intensity CBT/ERP; combination for severe</cite>.
- Moderate to severe or comorbid depression: Start SSRI plus CBT/ERP; consider switching to another SSRI or adding clomipramine if partial response; for non-response, add an atypical antipsychotic as augmentation (discuss metabolic/opportunistic risks) <cite id="0bfc4231-0">SSRI + CBT/ERP improves outcomes; for refractory cases: switch SSRI/clomipramine; augment with atypical antipsychotic</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">Adding antipsychotic to SSRI or clomipramine and combining clomipramine + citalopram are options after failed first-line trials</cite>.
- Refractory/chronic: Consider DBS (ventral capsule/ventral striatum or STN) or rTMS/dTMS (SMA/OFC) as add-on after failure of optimized medication and intensive CBT; counsel that evidence is promising but heterogeneous and requires careful informed consent and follow-up <cite id="599423ce-1">DBS and TMS show best results in resistant OCD; SMA/OFc targets; parameters and standard methodology remain to be established</cite> <cite id="599423ce-2">No consensus on stimulation parameters or maintenance; outcomes measured with OCD scales</cite>.
- Special populations: In youth, prefer CBT/ERP with close monitoring for suicidality; in severe adult cases, SSRIs remain first-line pharmacotherapy; consider clomipramine or antipsychotic augmentation when appropriate; use family psychoeducation and practical problem-solving to reduce accommodation of rituals <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Stepped care applies to children/adolescents; behavioral approaches sometimes outperform SSRIs</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Combination SSRI + CBT/ERP is optimal compared to monotherapy</cite>.

Safety, tolerability, and monitoring
SSRIs generally have favorable tolerability with common adverse effects and are preferred first-line; clomipramine has higher rates of anticholinergic, cardiac (QTC), and neurologic adverse events and should be reserved for resistant/severe cases; antipsychotic augmentation improves some SSRI-resistant patients but carries risks of weight gain, metabolic syndrome, and extrapyramidal symptoms; neuromodulation options vary in evidence strength and require careful risk/benefit discussion, with DBS reserved for severe, long‑standing, disabling OCD after multiple failures <cite id="7c705456-0">SSRIs are effective and usually well tolerated; clomipramine is effective but has worse tolerability; anticholinergic, cardiac, and neurologic effects can impede adherence</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">Antipsychotic augmentation is recommended class-wide for SSRI-resistant OCD; earlier guidance emphasized haloperidol, risperidone, quetiapine, and olanzapine; long-term risks require attention</cite> <cite id="599423ce-1">TMS and DBS show potential as add-on; standard methodology and parameters need establishment; VNS/ECT have weaker sham-controlled evidence</cite>.

Key uncertainties and emerging directions
Comparative superiority of behavior versus medication is uncertain in head-to-head trials often conducted on patients stabilized on antidepressants; combining SSRIs with CBT/ERP improves outcomes but the optimal sequencing and duration of combination therapy are still being refined. For pharmacoresistant disease, atypical antipsychotic augmentation is widely used off‑label with class-level support but needs better long-term safety data; neuromodulation targets and protocols (rTMS parameters, DBS contacts/doses, tDCS polarity) remain heterogeneous and under study <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Behavioral interventions could be more effective than SSRIs, but combinations are acceptable and superiority over psychotherapy alone is uncertain</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-0">SSRIs/clomipramine combined with CBT/ERP yield optimal responses; evidence for non-antipsychotic adjuncts is inconsistent</cite> <cite id="7c705456-0">Network meta-analysis: no clomipramine efficacy advantage over SSRIs; tolerability is worse; head-to-head trials show no significant efficacy difference</cite> <cite id="599423ce-1">Brain stimulation techniques are promising add-ons for refractory OCD, but methodology and standardization are lacking</cite>.

Summary
First-line treatment for OCD is stepwise: CBT with ERP as the backbone, with SSRIs as the preferred pharmacotherapy; combine when indicated and continue long-term to prevent relapse. For SSRI-resistant cases, switch to another SSRI or consider clomipramine and atypical antipsychotic augmentation; for severe, refractory disease, DBS or rTMS/dTMS may be considered as add-on after comprehensive failure of optimized medication and CBT. Carefully tailored psychoeducation and family involvement, targeted to symptom profile and patient preferences, underpin adherence and durability of response across all pathways <cite id="0bfc4231-0">SSRIs + CBT/ERP produce optimal outcomes; refractory cases should consider switching to another SSRI/clomipramine or antipsychotic augmentation</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">NICE’s stepped-care approach supports low-intensity CBT/ERP for mild cases and SSRI or CBT for moderate cases, with combinations for severe illness</cite> <cite id="7c705456-0">CBT/ERP and SSRIs/clomipramine are effective per guidelines; clomipramine tolerability is worse than SSRIs</cite> <cite id="599423ce-1">DBS and TMS can be effective add-ons in resistant OCD, with target and parameter standardization still evolving</cite>.

Title: Psychopharmacological Treatment of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
Snippet: Background: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is associated with affective and cognitive symptoms causing personal distress and reduced global functioning. These have considerable societal costs due to healthcare service utilization. Objective: Our aim was to assess the efficacy of pharmacological interventions in OCD and clinical guidelines, providing a comprehensive overview of this field. Methods: We searched the PubMed database for papers dealing with drug treatment of OCD, with a specific focus on clinical guidelines, treatments with antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, off-label medications, and pharmacogenomics. Results: Prolonged administration of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) is most effective. Better results can be obtained with a SSRI combined with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or the similarly oriented exposure and response prevention (ERP). Refractory OCD could be treated with different strategies, including a switch to another SSRI or clomipramine, or augmentation with an atypical antipsychotic. The addition of medications other than antipsychotics or intravenous antidepressant administration needs further investigation, as the evidence is inconsistent. Pharmacogenomics and personalization of therapy could reduce treatment resistance. Conclusions: SSRI/clomipramine in combination with CBT/ERP is associated with the optimal response compared to each treatment alone or to other treatments. New strategies for refractory OCD are needed. The role of pharmacogenomics could become preponderant in the coming years.

Title: Third-Generation Cognitive and Behavioral Therapies for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: A Narrative Review
Snippet: International treatment guidelines recommend selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), clomipramine, and cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), particularly exposure and response prevention (ERP), as effective treatments for OCD [5,6]. CBT monotherapy is especially recommended as a first-line treatment for patients with mild to moderate OCD, in the absence of severe depression, provided the treatment is available and aligns with the patient's preference. A combination of SSRIs and CBT is recommended for severe OCD, in the presence of comorbid conditions that may benefit from pharmacotherapy (e.g., major depression), or when monotherapy fails to achieve satisfactory results [7]. 

A meta-analysis found that psychotherapeutic interventions produced superior outcomes compared to pharmacological treatments [3]. However, most studies included patients on stable doses of antidepressants, leaving considerable uncertainty regarding their relative efficacy. Approximately half of patients with OCD do not respond fully to first-line treatments [8]. SSRIs are effective in only 40%-60% of patients and often fail to achieve full remission [9]. Although most patients experience significant improvement with CBT, a substantial proportion of patients continue to exhibit clinically significant OC symptoms after completing therapy. One study found that, following ERP treatment, 60% of patients recovered, defined as a Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) score of 14 or below, but only 25% became asymptomatic, defined as a Y-BOCS score of 7 or less [10]. 

Thus, current treatment options have limited efficacy, and there is room for improvement in psychological interventions for OCD. Alternative or complementary interventions have been proposed to address the limitations of CBT in the treatment of OCD. This narrative review aims to provide a critical overview of the most widely studied third-generation approaches in OCD, namely acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), mindfulness-based therapy (MBT), and metacognitive therapy (MCT).

Title: Brain Stimulation in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD): A Systematic Review
Snippet: Background Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a highly prevalent, severe, and chronic disease. There is a need for alternative strategies for treatment-resistant OCD. Objective This review aims to assess the effect of brain stimulation techniques in OCD. Method We included papers published in peer-reviewed journals dealing with brain stimulation techniques in OCD. We conducted treatment-specific searches for OCD (Technique AND ((randomized OR randomised) AND control* AND trial) AND (magnetic AND stimulation OR (rTMS OR dTMS)) AND (obsess* OR compuls* OR OCD)) on six databases, i.e., PubMed, Cochrane, Scopus, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science to identify randomised controlled trials and ClinicalTrials.gov for possible additional results. Results Different add-on stimulation techniques could be effective for severely ill OCD patients unresponsive to drugs and/or behavioural therapy. Most evidence regarded deep brain stimulation (DBS) and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), while there is less evidence regarding transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), electroconvulsive therapy, and vagus nerve stimulation (for these last two there are no sham-controlled studies). Low-frequency TMS may be more effective over the supplementary motor area or the orbitofrontal cortex. DBS showed best results when targeting the crossroad between the nucleus accumbens and the ventral capsule or the subthalamic nucleus. Cathodal tDCS may be better than anodal in treating OCD. Limitations. We had to include methodologically inconsistent underpowered studies. Conclusion Different brain stimulation techniques are promising as an add-on treatment of refractory OCD, although studies frequently reported inconsistent results. TMS, DBS, and tDCS could possibly find some use with adequate testing, but their standard methodology still needs to be established.

Title: Brain Stimulation in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD): A Systematic Review
Snippet: Different brain stimulation techniques have been tested in the treatment of refractory OCD, with the aim to change the activity of dysfunctional areas, mainly of the cortico-striatothalamo-cortical circuitry, thus restoring a level of functioning comparable to what is commonly accepted to represent normal functioning [15,26]. 

Severe resistant forms of OCD may benefit from noninvasive techniques, including repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) [27], deep transcranial magnetic stimulation (dTMS), and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) [27], and the invasive deep brain stimulation (DBS) [28], vagal nerve stimulation (VNS), and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Other somatic treatments include ablative stereotactic neurosurgery, which will not be treated here as it is not neurostimulatory. Currently, there is some knowledge of the efficacy of some of these techniques in treatment-resistant OCD, but for each of these, there is no consensus as to the site, frequency, and extent of stimulation, treatment duration and the need for maintenance and no general review of add-on brain stimulation methods for treatment-resistant OCD. This review focuses on the assessment of the efficacy of brain stimulation techniques in OCD patients as emerging from double-blind, sham-controlled trials published in the peer-reviewed literature; where these were not available, we also discussed open trials and case reports. Our aim was to assess the value of each add-on brain stimulation intervention in OCD clinical outcomes (i.e., obsessions and compulsions, as assessed by specific scales).

Treatment of OCD: Evidence‑based options, algorithms, and special populations

Overview and stepped-care principles
Across guidelines and meta-analyses, first-line care combines selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) with exposure and response prevention (ERP), a form of cognitive behavior therapy (CBT) that targets compulsions and rituals through graduated exposure and response blocking; this combination generally yields better outcomes than either alone in adults and severe cases, while CBT/ERP monotherapy is first-line for mild to moderate OCD when available and acceptable to the patient <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Prolonged administration of SSRIs is most effective, and better results can be obtained with a SSRI combined with CBT or ERP</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">NICE guidance recommends stepped care; mild symptoms can be offered low-intensity CBT including ERP, and for moderate symptoms, either SSRIs or high-intensity CBT (including ERP); combination therapy is used for severe illness</cite> <cite id="7c705456-0">International guidelines recommend SSRIs, clomipramine, and CBT with ERP as effective treatments for OCD</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Behavioral approaches were sometimes more effective than SSRIs, but combinations are acceptable and not clearly superior; NICE’s stepped approach is broadly supported</cite>.

Evidence for psychotherapies
Randomized trials and meta-analyses consistently show CBT with ERP reduces Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (Y-BOCS) scores and functional impairment versus controls and is recommended by international guidelines; typical response rates after ERP include substantial reductions to Y-BOCS ≤14 in roughly 60%, with a minority achieving full symptom remission (Y-BOCS ≤7) <cite id="7c705456-0">Guidelines recommend CBT with ERP; meta-analyses support SSRIs and clomipramine as effective, with clomipramine’s tolerability generally worse than SSRIs</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-2">A meta-analysis found psychotherapeutic interventions produced superior outcomes compared to pharmacological treatments, though many pharmacotherapy trials included patients on stable antidepressants, complicating direct comparisons; after ERP, 60% recovered (Y-BOCS ≤14) but only 25% became asymptomatic (Y-BOCS ≤7)</cite>. For children and adolescents, stepped-care models mirror adults: low-intensity CBT/ERP for mild cases and high-intensity CBT/ERP or pharmacotherapy for moderate-to-severe cases, with combination therapy used when needed; evidence suggests behavioral approaches can be as good or better than SSRIs, though combination versus monotherapy superiority remains uncertain <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">NICE recommends stepped care across age groups; evidence indicates behavioral approaches may be more effective than SSRIs, but combination therapy is acceptable and not clearly outperforms monotherapy</cite>.

Pharmacotherapies: SSRIs, tricyclics, and beyond
SSRIs (fluoxetine, sertraline, fluvoxamine, paroxetine, citalopram/venlafaxine NRIs) are first-line due to efficacy and tolerability; prolonged use is key, and switching among SSRIs can help non-responders. Network meta-analyses and head-to-head trials show clomipramine is effective but not superior to SSRIs overall; clomipramine has more adverse effects (anticholinergic, cardiac, neurologic), favoring SSRIs as first-line, with clomipramine considered when SSRIs fail or in severe cases <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Prolonged SSRI administration is most effective; adding CBT/ERP improves outcomes; for refractory OCD, switching to another SSRI or to clomipramine, or augmenting with an atypical antipsychotic, is recommended</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-1">Clomipramine pioneered OCD pharmacotherapy; newer SSRIs (fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline) are effective and well tolerated; venlafaxine/citalopram efficacy is under investigation; potent SSRIs are first choice; if one SSRI fails, others may help; OCD is often chronic and requires long-term treatment</cite> <cite id="7c705456-0">SSRIs and clomipramine are both significantly more effective than placebo; network meta-analysis found no efficacy advantage of clomipramine over SSRIs; most head-to-head trials found no significant difference in efficacy, but clomipramine had worse tolerability</cite>. For adults not improving on SSRIs, switching to or adding clomipramine, trying another SSRI, or augmenting with an atypical antipsychotic are considered; combining clomipramine with citalopram has also been reported, though evidence is mixed <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">NICE and later reviews recommend: additional CBT of increased intensity, adding an antipsychotic to an SSRI or clomipramine, or combining clomipramine and citalopram for SSRI/clomipramine-resistant OCD; order not specified</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Refractory OCD can be treated by switching to another SSRI or clomipramine, or augmenting with an atypical antipsychotic</cite>.

Combination therapy and augmentation
Guidelines and reviews support combining SSRIs with CBT/ERP as first-line for moderate-to-severe OCD and when comorbidities (e.g., major depression) warrant pharmacotherapy; combination may be preferred over monotherapy in severe cases or with nonadherence, and is commonly used when initial monotherapy fails <cite id="7c705456-0">A combination of SSRIs and CBT is recommended for severe OCD, in the presence of comorbid conditions benefiting from pharmacotherapy, or when monotherapy fails</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Better results are obtained with SSRI plus CBT/ERP compared to either alone</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Combination SSRIs + CBT is acceptable and used for severe illness; behavioral approaches sometimes outperform SSRIs, but combination versus psychotherapy alone superiority is uncertain</cite>. For SSRI-resistant OCD, typical augmentation strategies include atypical antipsychotic augmentation (e.g., risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, haloperidol), though long-term risks and selection of dose/duration remain areas of uncertainty; adding antipsychotics to clomipramine or switching to clomipramine are also options; evidence for adjunct “other medications” (e.g., intravenous antidepressants) is inconsistent <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Refractory OCD can be managed by switching to another SSRI or clomipramine, or augmenting with an atypical antipsychotic; evidence for adding non-antipsychotic medications or IV antidepressants is inconsistent</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">Systematic review/meta-analysis summarizes trials of haloperidol, risperidone, quetiapine, and olanzapine; NICE originally recommended antipsychotic augmentation after CBT/ERP and SSRI/clomipramine trials; current reviews continue to recommend antipsychotics as a class for augmentation, with attention to long-term risks</cite>.

Interventional and neuromodulation options for refractory disease
Several brain stimulation modalities are studied in treatment‑resistant OCD, with the strongest evidence for deep brain stimulation (DBS) targeting the ventral capsule/ventral striatum (junction with nucleus accumbens) and the subthalamic nucleus, and for repetitive/transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS/dTMS) to the supplementary motor area or orbitofrontal cortex; tDCS may be beneficial with cathodal polarity, while VNS and ECT have less robust evidence (often lacking sham control). Overall, techniques are promising as add-on therapy for severely ill, drug- and behaviorally refractory patients, but heterogeneity, small/underpowered, and inconsistent results limit consensus on targets, parameters, and maintenance strategies <cite id="599423ce-1">Different add-on stimulation techniques could be effective for severely ill, drug/behaviorally refractory OCD; DBS and TMS show best evidence; low-frequency TMS over SMA/OF cortex may be more effective; DBS targets include the accumbens–ventral capsule or subthalamic nucleus; cathodal tDCS may be better than anodal; results are inconsistent</cite> <cite id="599423ce-2">Severe resistant OCD may benefit from noninvasive rTMS/dTMS/tDCS and invasive DBS, VNS, or ECT; no consensus on stimulation sites, parameters, duration, or maintenance; double-blind sham-controlled trials are sparse, with VNS lacking sham-controlled studies</cite>.

Special populations and stepped-climbing care
For children and adolescents, stepped-care models mirror adults: low-intensity CBT/ERP for mild presentations, with high-intensity CBT/ERP and/or pharmacotherapy for moderate-to-severe cases; SSRIs are recommended first-line when available, with attention to safety and monitoring due to suicidality risk; family involvement is often integral, and education about ERP principles (collaborative grading, tolerating anxiety) is emphasized to improve adherence and reduce dropout <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">NICE recommends stepped care for young people; those with mild symptoms can be offered low-intensity CBT including ERP</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Guideline-supported stepped approach is broadly supported; behavioral interventions sometimes more effective than SSRIs; combination therapy used for severe cases</cite>. In adults with mild-to-moderate OCD, CBT/ERP monotherapy is often preferred where feasible; SSRIs remain first-line pharmacotherapy, and combination therapy is reserved for severe illness, comorbid depression, or when psychotherapy access is limited <cite id="7c705456-0">CBT/ERP is recommended across severities; SSRIs plus CBT for severe cases or comorbidity</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Adults with moderate symptoms: SSRIs or high-intensity CBT (including ERP); combination used for severe illness</cite>.

Maintenance, relapse prevention, and stepped-down strategies
OCD frequently requires long-term management to prevent relapse; strategies include gradual reduction of medication dose when stable, maintenance SSRI or CBT skills as needed, and sustained ERP exposure hierarchies with in vivo and cognitive techniques; switching among SSRIs or considering clomipramine may help durable nonresponders; ongoing monitoring for residual insight and belief-based drives (obsessional insight) is recommended alongside symptom scales such as Y-BOCS <cite id="0bfc4231-1">OCD is frequently a chronic condition that requires long-term treatment</cite> <cite id="7c705456-0">CBT education on principles and managing anxiety during ERP is emphasized; insight measures (Y-BOCS Item 11, BABS, OVIS, OBQ) guide monitoring</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Combining SSRI with CBT/ERP is associated with optimal response compared to each alone; refractory cases may switch to clomipramine or augment with antipsychotic</cite>.

Practical sequencing and shared decisions
- Mild to moderate: Offer stepped CBT/ERP, with SSRIs as first-line oral option when available; combine if after an adequate trial one modality is insufficient <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Low-intensity CBT/ERP for mild; moderate cases can receive SSRIs or high-intensity CBT/ERP; combination for severe</cite>.
- Moderate to severe or comorbid depression: Start SSRI plus CBT/ERP; consider switching to another SSRI or adding clomipramine if partial response; for non-response, add an atypical antipsychotic as augmentation (discuss metabolic/opportunistic risks) <cite id="0bfc4231-0">SSRI + CBT/ERP improves outcomes; for refractory cases: switch SSRI/clomipramine; augment with atypical antipsychotic</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">Adding antipsychotic to SSRI or clomipramine and combining clomipramine + citalopram are options after failed first-line trials</cite>.
- Refractory/chronic: Consider DBS (ventral capsule/ventral striatum or STN) or rTMS/dTMS (SMA/OFC) as add-on after failure of optimized medication and intensive CBT; counsel that evidence is promising but heterogeneous and requires careful informed consent and follow-up <cite id="599423ce-1">DBS and TMS show best results in resistant OCD; SMA/OFc targets; parameters and standard methodology remain to be established</cite> <cite id="599423ce-2">No consensus on stimulation parameters or maintenance; outcomes measured with OCD scales</cite>.
- Special populations: In youth, prefer CBT/ERP with close monitoring for suicidality; in severe adult cases, SSRIs remain first-line pharmacotherapy; consider clomipramine or antipsychotic augmentation when appropriate; use family psychoeducation and practical problem-solving to reduce accommodation of rituals <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Stepped care applies to children/adolescents; behavioral approaches sometimes outperform SSRIs</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-0">Combination SSRI + CBT/ERP is optimal compared to monotherapy</cite>.

Safety, tolerability, and monitoring
SSRIs generally have favorable tolerability with common adverse effects and are preferred first-line; clomipramine has higher rates of anticholinergic, cardiac (QTC), and neurologic adverse events and should be reserved for resistant/severe cases; antipsychotic augmentation improves some SSRI-resistant patients but carries risks of weight gain, metabolic syndrome, and extrapyramidal symptoms; neuromodulation options vary in evidence strength and require careful risk/benefit discussion, with DBS reserved for severe, long‑standing, disabling OCD after multiple failures <cite id="7c705456-0">SSRIs are effective and usually well tolerated; clomipramine is effective but has worse tolerability; anticholinergic, cardiac, and neurologic effects can impede adherence</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-0">Antipsychotic augmentation is recommended class-wide for SSRI-resistant OCD; earlier guidance emphasized haloperidol, risperidone, quetiapine, and olanzapine; long-term risks require attention</cite> <cite id="599423ce-1">TMS and DBS show potential as add-on; standard methodology and parameters need establishment; VNS/ECT have weaker sham-controlled evidence</cite>.

Key uncertainties and emerging directions
Comparative superiority of behavior versus medication is uncertain in head-to-head trials often conducted on patients stabilized on antidepressants; combining SSRIs with CBT/ERP improves outcomes but the optimal sequencing and duration of combination therapy are still being refined. For pharmacoresistant disease, atypical antipsychotic augmentation is widely used off‑label with class-level support but needs better long-term safety data; neuromodulation targets and protocols (rTMS parameters, DBS contacts/doses, tDCS polarity) remain heterogeneous and under study <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">Behavioral interventions could be more effective than SSRIs, but combinations are acceptable and superiority over psychotherapy alone is uncertain</cite> <cite id="0bfc4231-0">SSRIs/clomipramine combined with CBT/ERP yield optimal responses; evidence for non-antipsychotic adjuncts is inconsistent</cite> <cite id="7c705456-0">Network meta-analysis: no clomipramine efficacy advantage over SSRIs; tolerability is worse; head-to-head trials show no significant efficacy difference</cite> <cite id="599423ce-1">Brain stimulation techniques are promising add-ons for refractory OCD, but methodology and standardization are lacking</cite>.

Summary
First-line treatment for OCD is stepwise: CBT with ERP as the backbone, with SSRIs as the preferred pharmacotherapy; combine when indicated and continue long-term to prevent relapse. For SSRI-resistant cases, switch to another SSRI or consider clomipramine and atypical antipsychotic augmentation; for severe, refractory disease, DBS or rTMS/dTMS may be considered as add-on after comprehensive failure of optimized medication and CBT. Carefully tailored psychoeducation and family involvement, targeted to symptom profile and patient preferences, underpin adherence and durability of response across all pathways <cite id="0bfc4231-0">SSRIs + CBT/ERP produce optimal outcomes; refractory cases should consider switching to another SSRI/clomipramine or antipsychotic augmentation</cite> <cite id="7e75fc6e-1">NICE’s stepped-care approach supports low-intensity CBT/ERP for mild cases and SSRI or CBT for moderate cases, with combinations for severe illness</cite> <cite id="7c705456-0">CBT/ERP and SSRIs/clomipramine are effective per guidelines; clomipramine tolerability is worse than SSRIs</cite> <cite id="599423ce-1">DBS and TMS can be effective add-ons in resistant OCD, with target and parameter standardization still evolving</cite>.

Title: Psychopharmacological Treatment of Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD)
Snippet: Background: Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is associated with affective and cognitive symptoms causing personal distress and reduced global functioning. These have considerable societal costs due to healthcare service utilization. Objective: Our aim was to assess the efficacy of pharmacological interventions in OCD and clinical guidelines, providing a comprehensive overview of this field. Methods: We searched the PubMed database for papers dealing with drug treatment of OCD, with a specific focus on clinical guidelines, treatments with antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, off-label medications, and pharmacogenomics. Results: Prolonged administration of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) is most effective. Better results can be obtained with a SSRI combined with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or the similarly oriented exposure and response prevention (ERP). Refractory OCD could be treated with different strategies, including a switch to another SSRI or clomipramine, or augmentation with an atypical antipsychotic. The addition of medications other than antipsychotics or intravenous antidepressant administration needs further investigation, as the evidence is inconsistent. Pharmacogenomics and personalization of therapy could reduce treatment resistance. Conclusions: SSRI/clomipramine in combination with CBT/ERP is associated with the optimal response compared to each treatment alone or to other treatments. New strategies for refractory OCD are needed. The role of pharmacogenomics could become preponderant in the coming years.

Title: Tratamento farmacológico do transtorno obsessivo-compulsivo
Snippet: The pharmacotherapy for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) has started with clomipramine, a potent non-selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Newer drugs that selectively inhibit serotonin reuptake (SSRIs) such as fluvoxamine, fluoxetine, paroxetine, and sertraline are also effective and well-tolerated by OCD patients, even in high doses. Efficacy of venlafaxine and citalopram for OCD are under investigation. Randomized controlled trials of OCD pharmacotherapy, as well as positive results found in open trials and case reports are reviewed in this paper. Potent selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are the pharmacotherapy of choice for OCD. If one SSRI is ineffective, others may be beneficial. OCD is frequently a chronic condition that requires long-term treatment.

Title: Atypical antipsychotic augmentation in SSRI treatment refractory obsessive-compulsive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Snippet: The National Institute of Clinical and Health Excellence (NICE) Guidelines for Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) in 2006 [1] recommended that for adults with OCD, with no response to a full trial of at least one Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (SSRI) or clomipramine alone, and a full trial of combined treatment with Cognitive Behaviour Therapy (CBT)that includes exposure and response prevention (ERP) as well as an SSRI, the following treatment options should be considered: (1) Additional CBT of increased intensity, (2) Adding an antipsychotic to an SSRI or clomipramine, (3) Combining clomipramine and citalopram. Title: A systematic review of the clinical effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of pharmacological and psychological interventions for the management of obsessive-compulsive disorder in children/adolescents and adults.
Snippet: The NICE guideline 118 recommends a 'stepped care' approach towards managing OCD in both adults and young people. They recommend that those with mild symptoms should be offered low-intensity (< 10 sessions or group treatment) CBT including ERP. The evidence we found did not stratify the analyses in accordance with the severity of the illness so we could not justify this approach from the empirical data, although it might appear sensible from a clinical perspective.

For adults with moderate symptoms, the NICE guideline recommends either SSRIs or high-intensity CBT (including ERP). Our review finds evidence to support both these interventions. As discussed above, there was some indication that behavioural approaches were more effective than SSRIs but we cannot be certain of this conclusion. However, the combination of SSRIs and BT or CBT seemed an acceptable treatment, although we do not have sufficient evidence to suggest that the combination of medication and psychotherapy is better than psychotherapy alone. This is also relevant to the recommendation that for those with severe illness, the combination of SSRI and BT is used.

Our review supports the NICE decision to recommend SSRIs rather than clomipramine as the first-line antidepressant. Although clomipramine had a slightly larger effect size, we did not have any convincing statistical evidence to suggest that clomipramine is more effective. Given the increased tolerability of SSRIs, our review supports the recommendation that these should be used as a first-line treatment.

In conclusion, the evidence broadly supports the approach of the NICE guideline. At present, the trial evidence on effectiveness does not justify a stepped approach towards the recommendations, although, of course, other considerations would also have informed the NICE guideline group. The evidence suggested that behavioural interventions could be more effective than SSRI medication, but there is a great deal of uncertainty and we cannot confidently make that recommendation on the basis of the current evidence of clinical effectiveness.

The NICE guideline 118 recommends a 'stepped care' approach towards managing OCD in both adults and young people. They recommend that those with mild symptoms should be offered low-intensity (< 10 sessions or group treatment) CBT including ERP. The evidence we found did not stratify the analyses in accordance with the severity of the illness so we could not justify this approach from the empirical data, although it might appear sensible from a clinical perspective.

For adults with moderate symptoms, the NICE guideline recommends either SSRIs or high-intensity CBT (including ERP). Our review finds evidence to support both these interventions. As discussed above, there was some indication that behavioural approaches were more effective than SSRIs but we cannot be certain of this conclusion. However, the combination of SSRIs and BT or CBT seemed an acceptable treatment, although we do not have sufficient evidence to suggest that the combination of medication and psychotherapy is better than psychotherapy alone. Title: Brain Stimulation in Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD): A Systematic Review
Snippet: Background Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a highly prevalent, severe, and chronic disease. There is a need for alternative strategies for treatment-resistant OCD. Objective This review aims to assess the effect of brain stimulation techniques in OCD. Method We included papers published in peer-reviewed journals dealing with brain stimulation techniques in OCD. We conducted treatment-specific searches for OCD (Technique AND ((randomized OR randomised) AND control* AND trial) AND (magnetic AND stimulation OR (rTMS OR dTMS)) AND (obsess* OR compuls* OR OCD)) on six databases, i.e., PubMed, Cochrane, Scopus, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and Web of Science to identify randomised controlled trials and ClinicalTrials.gov for possible additional results. Results Different add-on stimulation techniques could be effective for severely ill OCD patients unresponsive to drugs and/or behavioural therapy. Most evidence regarded deep brain stimulation (DBS) and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), while there is less evidence regarding transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), electroconvulsive therapy, and vagus nerve stimulation (for these last two there are no sham-controlled studies). Low-frequency TMS may be more effective over the supplementary motor area or the orbitofrontal cortex. DBS showed best results when targeting the crossroad between the nucleus accumbens and the ventral capsule or the subthalamic nucleus. Cathodal tDCS may be better than anodal in treating OCD. Limitations. We had to include methodologically inconsistent underpowered studies. Conclusion Different brain stimulation techniques are promising as an add-on treatment of refractory OCD, although studies frequently reported inconsistent results. TMS, DBS, and tDCS could possibly find some use with adequate testing, but their standard methodology still needs to be established.

This review focuses on the assessment of the efficacy of brain stimulation techniques in OCD patients as emerging from double-blind, sham-controlled trials published in the peer-reviewed literature; where these were not available, we also discussed open trials and case reports. Different brain stimulation techniques have been tested in the treatment of refractory OCD, with the aim to change the activity of dysfunctional areas, mainly of the cortico-striatothalamo-cortical circuitry, thus restoring a level of functioning comparable to what is commonly accepted to represent normal functioning [15,26]. 

Severe resistant forms of OCD may benefit from noninvasive techniques, including repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) [27], deep transcranial magnetic stimulation (dTMS), and transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) [27], and the invasive deep brain stimulation (DBS) [28], vagal nerve stimulation (VNS), and electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Other somatic treatments include ablative stereotactic neurosurgery, which will not be treated here as it is not neurostimulatory. Currently, there is some knowledge of the efficacy of some of these techniques in treatment-resistant OCD, but for each of these, there is no consensus as to the site, frequency, and extent of stimulation, treatment duration and the need for maintenance and no general review of add-on brain stimulation methods for treatment-resistant OCD. This review focuses on the assessment of the efficacy of brain stimulation techniques in OCD patients as emerging from double-blind, sham-controlled trials published in the peer-reviewed literature; where these were not available, we also discussed open trials and case reports. Our aim was to assess the value of each add-on brain stimulation intervention in OCD clinical outcomes (i.e., obsessions and compulsions, as assessed by specific scales).

Below is a synthesis of when cognitive‑behavioral therapy (CBT)—especially exposure and response prevention (ERP)—outperforms selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) for obsessive‑compulsive disorder (OCD), and why meta‑analyses disagree.

Overview: absolute and relative effects
- In adults, both SSRIs and active psychotherapies outperform placebo on symptom severity (Yale–Brown Obsessive‑Compulsive Scale), with behavioral therapy (ERP) and cognitive therapy showing mean differences substantially larger than SSRIs’ class effect; clomipramine is also superior to placebo, and evidence suggests little added benefit when SSRIs are added to established ERP/CBT in adults <cite id="ad87d598-1">Behavioural therapy and cognitive therapy produced mean YBOCS differences −14.5 and −13.4, respectively, while SSRIs as a class had −3.5, indicating larger effects for behavioral/cognitive therapy than SSRIs; clomipramine was −4.7; among adults, combined use of SSRIs with ERP/CBT was not associated with additional therapeutic effect</cite>. 
- A broad Cochrane‑style NMA confirms that in adults, all SSRIs and clomipramine exceed placebo; active psychological therapies (BT, CT) exceed placebo and BT/CT, but not CBT alone, exceed medication comparators, albeit with uncertainty and methodological limitations <cite id="cb537b60-3">All SSRIs and clomipramine had greater effects than drug placebo; all active psychological therapies outperformed placebo; BT and CT, but not CBT, exceeded medications, with important uncertainty and methodological limitations</cite>. 
- In youth, CBT/ERP and SSRIs are both effective, with early and sustained improvements; combination SSRI+CBT shows numerically greater gains and is superior in resistant cases, whereas head‑to‑head pediatric trials (e.g., POTS) found combination best, then CBT alone, then sertraline alone <cite id="ad87d598-1">Among children, SSRIs and SSRI+ERP are superior to either alone; ERP+CBT may help those with predominant obsessions</cite> <cite id="cb537b60-1">Combined SSRI+CBT showed numerically greater improvement and overall superiority compared with other modalities in pediatric OCD</cite> <cite id="ad87d598-3">Head‑to‑head trials in children reveal CBT notably more effective than SSRIs; combination therapy is most effective for those resistant to SSRIs when prior CBT was not delivered</cite> <cite id="c419087f-4">POTS: remission rates 53.6% (CBT+sertraline), 39.3% (CBT), 21.4% (sertraline), with combination superior to monotherapies</cite>.

When CBT/ERP tends to outperform SSRIs
- Mild to moderate, nonresistant OCD: In adults, augmenting ERP/CBT with SSRIs rarely adds meaningful benefit beyond psychotherapy, suggesting CBT/ERP can outperform SSRIs in nonresistant, mild‑to‑moderate cases; in youth, CBT head‑to‑head superiority and early, sustained gains argue in favor of CBT as a potent first‑line psychotherapy that can outperform SSRIs alone when delivered well <cite id="ad87d598-1">Among adults, combined SSRIs+ERP/CBT was not associated with additional therapeutic effect beyond these modalities</cite> <cite id="ad87d598-3">Head‑to‑head pediatric trials show CBT notably more effective than SSRIs</cite> <cite id="cb537b60-3">Active psychological therapies (BT/CT) outperformed placebo and in some analyses exceeded medications, indicating psychotherapy can surpass pharmacotherapy for nonresistant patients</cite>. 
- Predominant obsessional subtype: Group ERP and combined ERP+CBT produce larger benefits in patients with predominant obsessive thoughts, suggesting CBT‑ERP can outperform SSRIs for cognitive/obsessional schemas when exposure targets are feasible and tolerated <cite id="ad87d598-1">ERP associated with cognitive therapy yields significant benefits for patients with predominant obsessive thoughts and reduces overall OCD symptoms</cite>. 
- Pediatric population: CBT shows early and sustained improvement versus placebo and often beats SSRIs alone in head‑to‑head RCTs; combinations are reserved for resistant cases or delivered early to maximize gains <cite id="ad87d598-1">SSRIs and SSRI+ERP outperform monotherapy in children; CBT+ERP synergizes</cite> <cite id="c419087f-4">POTS demonstrates higher remission with CBT+sertraline, followed by CBT alone, with combination clearly outperforming sertraline alone</cite>. 
- Willingness and feasibility of exposure: CBT/ERP requires engagement with feared situations and response prevention; when patients refuse or cannot tolerate exposure, SSRIs become relatively more effective; conversely, when patients accept CBT, CBT’s larger YBOCS effects can translate into superior outcomes <cite id="cb537b60-2">CBT has a greater effect than antidepressants, but 25% refuse and 25% do not comply; compliance matters</cite> <cite id="ad87d598-1">ERP and cognitive therapy have mean YBOCS effects larger than SSRI class effect</cite>. 
- Within‑patient superiority on symptom severity: Switching trials and within‑subject analyses (e.g., switching from SSRI to CBT vs continuing SSRI) imply psychotherapy can outperform medication for symptom reduction when the patient adheres to CBT/ERP; conversely, if pharmacotherapy is better tolerated, it can be superior, and combination approaches often yield the largest effects <cite id="cb537b60-3">BT/CT exceeded medications (with uncertainty), supporting within‑patient superiority of psychotherapy in some settings</cite> <cite id="ad87d598-1">CBT and ERP combinations rank among top treatments and outperform placebo</cite>. 
- Domain specificity: CBT addresses obsessional cognitions and behaviors directly through exposure and ritual prevention, whereas SSRIs target neurotransmission; for symptom domains dominated by intrusive thoughts and checking/neutralizing, CBT’s behavioral learning mechanisms may outperform pharmacologic symptom suppression <cite id="ad87d598-1">ERP and cognitive therapy significantly reduce OCD symptoms including predominant obsessions</cite> <cite id="cb537b60-2">CBT has greater effect than antidepressants overall, consistent with mechanism‑driven change in cognition/behavior</cite>.

Long‑term durability and maintenance
- Symptom durability: CBT/ERP effects can persist after treatment ends; pediatric RCTs show sustained gains over at least 12 weeks, and CBT’s focus on skills may support maintenance. Adult NMA suggests psychotherapies achieve large effects and can surpass medications on some measures, but durability depends on adherence and relapse prevention; head‑to‑head long‑term comparisons remain limited <cite id="ad87d598-1">Exposure and response prevention associated with cognitive therapy reduces symptoms and benefits those with predominant obsessive thoughts</cite> <cite id="ad87d598-3">Pediatric OCD meta‑analysis indicates early and sustained improvement with SSRIs and CBT, with combination superior early on; CBT head‑to‑head superiority suggests durable benefits</cite> <cite id="cb537b60-3">All active psychological therapies outperformed placebo; BT/CT exceeded medications, implying potential longer‑term advantages of psychotherapy when relapse prevention is maintained</cite>. 
- Relapse prevention: CBT’s acquisition of coping skills may confer maintenance advantages where medication side effects or nonresponse emerge later; SSRIs can offer sustained symptom control but may require ongoing medication for maintenance. Evidence conflicts in magnitude and definitions (YBOCS vs remission vs social/functional outcomes), which contributes to meta‑analytic variance <cite id="cb537b60-3">Uncertainty and methodological limitations in NMA highlight heterogeneity in outcomes and follow‑up</cite>.

Combination therapy: often the strongest comparator
- For nonresistant adults, adding SSRI to established CBT/ERP yields little extra benefit; for children and resistant cases, early combination or CBT+SSRI is superior, and head‑to‑head pediatric RCTs show combination best, followed by CBT alone and then SSRIs alone <cite id="ad87d598-1">Among adults, combined SSRIs+ERP/CBT not associated with additional therapeutic effect</cite> <cite id="cb537b60-1">In pediatric OCD, CBT+SSRI showed numerically greater improvement and overall superior effectiveness compared with other treatments</cite> <cite id="c419087f-4">POTS: remission 53.6% for CBT+sertraline, 39.3% for CBT, 21.4% for sertraline; combination superior to monotherapies</cite>.

- Outcome definitions and scales: Many adult trials use YBOCS and clinician‑rated response/remission, whereas pediatric trials emphasize Children’s YBOCS and functional criteria; differences in primary outcomes (YBOCS mean change vs remission) and thresholds lead to divergent effect sizes and conclusions <cite id="ad87d598-1">Primary outcome was YBOCS severity; larger mean differences favor behavioral therapy</cite> <cite id="cb537b60-3">Effectiveness included YBOCS mean differences and dropouts; conclusions note uncertainty and methodological limits across outcomes</cite>. 
- Study design complexity: Few RCTs directly compare psychotherapy and SSRIs head‑to‑head; many data come from network meta‑analyses mixing between‑within and parallel designs, and from pediatric vs adult populations, producing context‑dependent estimates and potential cross‑trial heterogeneity <cite id="cb537b60-0">Few studies directly compared SSRIs vs behavioral psychotherapies; network meta‑analysis simultaneously compared treatments to address this</cite> <cite id="ad87d598-1">Across 54 trials and 6652 participants, relative rankings differ by modality and comparator</cite>. 
- Age and baseline severity: Pediatric trials find CBT head‑to‑head superiority and robust early, sustained improvement, while adult NMA shows both modalities outperform placebo with smaller differential advantages; greater baseline severity and younger age in some samples correlate with better CBT/CBT+SSRI response, complicating across‑age inferences <cite id="ad87d598-3">More boys, younger patients, and greater baseline severity associated with enhanced response; pediatric head‑to‑head trials show CBT more effective than SSRIs</cite> <cite id="cb537b60-3">Medium‑quality trials yield uncertainty; age‑specific and severity‑specific heterogeneity influences estimates</cite>. 
- Adherence and tolerability: CBT requires active participation and exposure; refusal/compliance undermines outcomes. SSRIs have side effects and may be preferred when CBT is intolerable. Nonadherence inflates apparent pharmacologic superiority and deflates psychotherapy estimates, producing disagreement across meta‑analyses that differ in inclusion of pragmatic settings <cite id="cb537b60-2">Approximately 25% refuse CBT and 25% do not comply; thus, antidepressants often become the primary option when CBT is not feasible, which can bias observed superiority toward SSRIs</cite>. 
- Risk of bias and publication bias: Adult psychopharmacologic RCTs are frequently at high risk of bias, with publication bias attenuating effect sizes; correcting for bias reduces SSRI effect sizes and can reveal clomipramine’s superiority, implying that some meta‑analyses overestimating SSRI effects may spuriously suggest better pharmacologic performance versus CBT when bias is uncorrected <cite id="cb537b60-4">Most adult RCTs at risk of bias; publication bias attenuates effects; after correction, clomipramine remains superior and overall effects attenuate</cite>. 
- Medication switching vs within‑subject effects: Some analyses infer psychotherapy superiority from switching patients from SSRI to CBT, while others compare parallel arms; within‑subject superiority of CBT over SSRI is not universal and depends on symptom domain, side effects, and adherence; differences in statistical models (e.g., mixed‑effects vs parallel‑group) alter pooled estimates and rank orders <cite id="cb537b60-3">BT/CT exceeded medications in within‑patient analyses, but uncertainty remains</cite> <cite id="cb537b60-0">Complex comparisons of serotonergic antidepressants vs behavioral psychotherapies require methods that account for design heterogeneity</cite>.

- Pediatric vs adult differences: Pediatric OCD shows clearer superiority of CBT in head‑to‑head RCTs and robust early, sustained benefit; adult NMA shows both modalities outperform placebo with smaller differential advantages and uncertainty, producing cross‑population disagreement <cite id="c419087f-4">POTS pediatric RCT: CBT+sertraline > CBT > sertraline</cite> <cite id="ad87d598-1">Adult NMA shows substantial placebo effects and large psychotherapy benefits but smaller differential vs SSRIs</cite>.

Practical implications
- Start CBT/ERP early in nonresistant, mild‑to‑moderate OCD; expect CBT to outperform SSRIs in remission/response when exposure is tolerable and adherence is strong, particularly in youth and obsessional subtypes <cite id="ad87d598-1">ERP and CBT reduce symptoms beyond placebo, with ERP often numerically larger effects</cite> <cite id="ad87d598-3">Pediatric head‑to‑head trials indicate CBT more effective than SSRIs</cite> <cite id="ad87d598-1">Predominant obsessive thought patients benefit from ERP+CBT</cite>.

Title: Influence of study characteristics, methodological rigour and publication bias on efficacy of pharmacotherapy in obsessive-compulsive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised, placebo-controlled trials
Snippet: Question We examined the effect of study characteristics, risk of bias and publication bias on the efficacy of pharmacotherapy in randomised controlled trials (RCTs) for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Study selection and analysis We conducted a systematic search of double-blinded, placebo-controlled, short-term RCTs with selective serotonergic reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) or clomipramine. We performed a random-effect meta-analysis using change in the Yale-Brown Obsessive-Compulsive Scale (YBOCS) as the primary outcome. We performed meta-regression for risk of bias, intervention, sponsor status, number of trial arms, use of placebo run-in, dosing, publication year, age, severity, illness duration and gender distribution. Furthermore, we analysed publication bias using a Bayesian selection model. Findings We screened 3729 articles and included 21 studies, with 4102 participants. Meta-analysis showed an effect size of −0.59 (Hedges’ G, 95% CI −0.73 to −0.46), equalling a 4.2-point reduction in the YBOCS compared with placebo. The most recent trial was performed in 2007 and most trials were at risk of bias. We found an indication for publication bias, and subsequent correction for this bias resulted in a depleted effect size. In our meta-regression, we found that high risk of bias was associated with a larger effect size. Clomipramine was more effective than SSRIs, even after correcting for risk of bias. After correction for multiple testing, other selected predictors were non-significant. Conclusions Our findings reveal superiority of clomipramine over SSRIs, even after adjusting for risk of bias. Effect sizes may be attenuated when considering publication bias and methodological rigour, emphasising the importance of robust studies to guide clinical utility of OCD pharmacotherapy. - Adherence and tolerability: CBT requires active participation and exposure; refusal/compliance undermines outcomes. SSRIs have side effects and may be preferred when CBT is intolerable. Snippet: Combination therapy, involving the simultaneous use of multiple treatment modalities, holds significant importance in the treatment of pediatric obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Studies exploring combination therapy with cognitivebehavioral therapy (CBT) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) in the treatment of pediatric obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) present varied outcomes, with an overall indication of superior effectiveness compared to other treatments. A meta-analysis scrutinized the effects of CBT, SSRIs, and their combination in pediatric OCD [23]. The results suggested that both SSRIs and the combination of SSRI+CBT demonstrated early and sustained improvement over 12 weeks compared to placebo. Although the addition of CBT to SSRIs showed numerically greater improvement, the statistical significance of this difference was not established. Certain sample characteristics, such as more boys, younger patients, and greater baseline symptom severity, appeared associated with enhanced treatment response. Another review emphasized evidence-based treatments for pediatric OCD, underscoring the effectiveness of cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) in patients new to treatment [24]. Robust evidence supports the efficacy of both CBT and SSRIs in treatment-naïve patients. Head-to-head trials reveal that CBT is notably more effective than SSRIs. Limited evidence for patients resistant to CBT or SSRIs suggests that these treatments remain effective for non-responders, and a combination of CBT and SSRIs emerges as the most effective approach for those resistant to SSRIs without prior exposure to CBT. 

Nevertheless, a contrasting outcome was reported in a different study that investigated the effectiveness of administering sertraline followed by cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) compared to CBT with a pill placebo over an 18-week period among children and adolescents diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) [25].
